name: Sara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead an electricity company crew that builds and repairs power lines. My two-year technical diploma helps with the drawings, and I use AI every day to group customer reports before we take the truck out. I like finding the fault that a neat map missed, then showing a younger worker how to prove it with a meter. My partner and I have grown children; retirement is becoming a real conversation, though we have not fixed a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that small AI gains look like the report sorter I already use. The tool can group calls, but it cannot tell whether a broken span is isolated until we test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our typical lineworker wage and a few months of savings make present work manageable. I want a retirement estimate before promising a finish date, and this modest AI picture gives me no reason to hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repair shifts and compare grouped reports with our field readings. This year my partner and I would request a retirement income estimate and place it next to our regular household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about pay and curious about the software. An AI outage group can look complete while the meter shows two broken power line spans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you split grouped reports?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If two callers sound close but the voltage readings point to separate spans, I would split the cases in the tool. The next crew should not inherit a false single outage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a low retirement estimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid line shifts and review the date with my partner. Several months of savings do not replace a long run of wages.

say: I **use** AI daily to group outage calls while crews still test the actual line.
A **suggested** fault location must agree with field readings.
think: **Typical** pay and several months saved make current work manageable.
**Retirement** timing stays open until income estimates meet household costs.
do: **Keep** crew lead shifts and compare grouped calls with meter readings.
**Request** retirement income estimate and review it with partner.
feel: **Calm** about income and interested in modest software gains.
S0.quote: An AI outage group can look complete while the meter shows two broken power line spans.
fieldNote: She **uses** AI daily and actively corrects its groupings with field tests.
She requests **retirement** facts before choosing a finish date and does not treat several months of cash as lifetime income.

steps.text: Keep lead shifts and verify grouped reports with meter readings
Request retirement income estimate before choosing finish date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say stronger AI booking and buying could reduce wasted truck trips, and I would try a new outage routing tool early. The company should let field crews mark a wrong route without being punished for a slower number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office feels the first change, not my hands on a damaged line. My own pay looks steady for now, but a bad route score might squeeze the time we have to teach newer workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the routing tool’s correction controls on a paid shift and compare its first twenty suggestions with actual truck access. In the first year I would give the dispatcher the wrong gate locations and ask whether the corrected route reaches the next crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, with a small worry about targets. An AI route that ends at a footpath leaves a line truck no closer to the broken pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What route error would matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A map might choose a narrow footpath where our line truck cannot pass. I would record the actual service gate and travel time before the dispatcher sends another crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask to review the correction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the dispatcher and the crew lead who took the next callout to compare maps. If the wrong gate is still there, I would report it again with the work order number.

say: I would **test** new AI outage routing against actual line truck access.
**Field** corrections should reach the next crew without hurting workers’ targets.
think: **Office** tasks change first, while my own lineworker wage appears steady.
**Bad** route scores could reduce paid time for teaching newer workers.
do: **Learn** routing correction controls on a paid shift.
**Compare** twenty suggested routes with actual truck gates.
**Send** wrong gate locations to dispatcher and check later corrections.
feel: **Interested** in routing gains, slightly uneasy about targets.
S1.quote: An AI route that ends at a footpath leaves a line truck no closer to the broken pole.
fieldNote: She **tries** a new AI routing function promptly, consistent with daily tool use.
Her **concern** is quality of field correction and apprentice time, not an invented immediate pay cut.

steps.text: Learn AI routing correction controls during paid shift
Compare twenty AI routes with actual truck access

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full thinking AI by 2028 could plan nearly every callout when I am sixty, and capable robots around 2031 could do line repairs when I am sixty-three. I would volunteer for paid field trials with a crew stop control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot taking the ordinary callouts could shrink my hours before I know whether retirement income is enough. We have one to six months saved and some nearby line jobs, so I can respond, but I cannot ignore a possible wage gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply this year for a paid company robot field trial with written stop authority. In the first year after 2028 I would learn the robot controls on paid shifts, then compare actual callout earnings with household costs before deciding whether to seek a posted field tester role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the speed, even while I want to try the machine. A robot lifting a power line once tells me nothing about its grip on a split crossarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test on a damaged pole?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test whether the robot notices a split crossarm before gripping it. A crew member should be able to stop the movement and record the fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you seek the tester job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if callout earnings fall and a posted field tester role pays enough for our household. I would keep line shifts until a written offer exists.

say: **Thinking** AI reaches plans by 2028, with capable line robots around 2031.
I would **volunteer** for paid field trials with worker stop controls.
think: **Ordinary** callout loss could create a wage gap before retirement income is known.
**Several** months saved and some nearby work give choices, not certainty.
do: **Apply** for paid company field trial with written stop authority this year.
**Learn** robot controls during paid trial shifts after 2028.
**Seek** posted field tester role only if callout earnings fall and pay covers costs.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss, eager to test with safe controls.
S2.quote: A robot lifting a power line once tells me nothing about its grip on a split crossarm.
fieldNote: She **willingly** trains on controls during paid shifts, with written stop authority.
A **different** job is conditional on actual earnings loss and a posted adequate offer.

steps.text: Learn robot controls during paid trial with written stop authority
Seek posted field tester role if callout pay falls and offer covers costs
Keep line shifts until suitable written offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2031 changes dispatch when I am sixty-three, and capable robots around 2034 reach the line when I am sixty-six. The longer lead lets us train people to check robot repairs before a machine works alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My diploma and field work could suit a paid robot verifier role, but I do not want to trade a typical wage for an unpaid course. Retirement may be near, yet I need an actual income estimate before deciding whether to stay or leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company this year for a verifier course syllabus, paid hours and a posted local salary. If hands-on training is funded and a local verifier role pays at least my current wage, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when the post opens; otherwise I would keep repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of future wages but glad to have time to test a real path. I would want the course to show a failed line repair, not only a polished demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What failure belongs in the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice job should include a cracked crossarm hidden behind a wet cable. A robot verifier should find the wrong pole tag before the power line repair gets a clean signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a distant verifier role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a written wage and travel time with our household costs before deciding. Some nearby jobs exist, so I would not move for an unposted possibility.

say: The **extra** years allow funded field verification before robots reach lines around 2034.
I would **want** failure cases in the course.
think: A **paid** verifier post might fit my diploma if salary remains adequate.
**Retirement** cannot be chosen from a vague income estimate or an unpaid course.
do: **Request** funded verifier course and local posted salary details this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if hands-on course paid and local role matches wage.
**Apply** when posted local verifier role pays at least current rate.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss, able to inspect an actual training route.
S3.quote: A robot verifier should find the wrong pole tag before the power line repair gets a clean signature.
fieldNote: She **needs** funded hands-on study tied to a real local vacancy with current-rate pay.
The **slower** date allows evidence gathering without implying a guaranteed retirement age.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if funded hands-on course and local matching-pay role posted
Apply for posted local verifier role if pay matches current wage
Keep repair shifts if paid verifier route does not appear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2036 reaches the depot at sixty-eight for me, and capable robots around 2039 reach lines at seventy-one. A decade gives apprentices time to learn real fault checks before relying on a machine plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may have left full-time line work by then if the retirement income covers our costs. Several months of savings alone will not fund many years away, so the year of leaving remains open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the repair rota and request a retirement income estimate each year. If the figure covers household costs before 2036, I would leave full-time line work then; if it does not, I would apply for a posted paid field training role with hours I can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the technology dates, still careful with the retirement sums. I can choose after seeing the actual figures rather than promising a date now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the field training role involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice should find the broken power line before trusting the AI fault map that points elsewhere. I would need written paid hours for regular teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the offered teaching hours are too few?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe repair shifts or compare other nearby paid roles. I would not leave the crew until the combined household income meets our costs.

say: A **decade** lets apprentices learn field fault checks before robots arrive around 2039.
I would **teach** how to challenge an AI map with real measurements.
think: An **earlier** exit is possible only if retirement income covers household costs.
**Several** months saved alone cannot support an open-ended retirement.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and update retirement estimate annually.
**Leave** full-time line job before 2036 only if income covers household costs.
**Apply** for posted paid field trainer role if retirement income falls short.
feel: **Calm** about distant robots, cautious about retirement arithmetic.
S4.quote: An apprentice should find the broken power line before trusting the AI fault map that points elsewhere.
fieldNote: Her **conditional** exit is an actual leave-job decision, not merely an information request.
A **fallback** teaching role needs a posted paid position with workable hours.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and update retirement estimate annually
Leave full-time line job before 2036 if income covers household costs
Apply for posted paid field trainer role if retirement income short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots around 2031 could shrink callout wages before my partner and I know what retirement income will cover. Paid field trials, crew stop controls and a posted verifier salary would help. I will test a line robot on a damaged pole, but I will not make our household the unpaid test site.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether new lineworkers can still learn to recognise a false AI map before a machine makes the repair. My diploma helps, but most of my judgment came from site mistakes we caught early. A trainee needs paid time beside someone who can stop the work.

headlineQuote: I will test a line robot on a damaged pole, but I will not make our household the unpaid test site.
portrait: **Sara** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma who uses AI daily to group outage reports.
**Typical** pay, one to six months saved and some nearby line jobs support her and her partner as retirement approaches.
She **trials** new routing and robot controls early, but demands paid time and field stop authority before accepting tool claims.
She **may** train for a funded verifier job or leave full-time work if actual retirement income covers the household.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031 and reduce callout wages before retirement income is known.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** field trials, crew stop controls and a real verifier salary would help her weigh continued work.
